narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically denied your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. At 28.5, it sits well below the average of 37.2 among students who were accepted, signaling weaker preparation in the eyes of the model. Your undergraduate GPA came next and worked in your favor; at 3.4 it is actually higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students, helping to pull the prediction back toward passing. Finally, your first-year law school grades also pulled the prediction downward. Placing in the 5th decile rather than the 6th-decile average of accepted students made the model slightly less confident in your long-term success.

Taken together, the negative impact of the lower LSAT outweighed the positive effects of your stronger GPA and solid first-year performance, resulting in a failure prediction just over the threshold.

You should focus on strengthening your LSAT performance through targeted preparation, as this was the dominant factor. Retaking the test with a higher score would likely change the model’s outlook and improve your chances on a future application.
